name: Getting started with Moksy
description: Turn your first idea into a build-ready plan.

groups.idea: element of a good idea brief

cards.subject: A Moksy project
says: holds one idea and its document
is created by a customer to start working on an idea
cards.use: want to know where one idea and its document live
not: holds every customer's ideas in one shared place

cards.subject: The Moksy interview
says: has an AI ask a series of questions about your idea
supplies the answers that the document is built from
cards.use: need the stage where you answer questions about your idea
not: is a live video call with a human reviewer

cards.subject: The output document
says: is built from your interview answers
is the plan for your idea
cards.use: want the thing you receive once the interview is finished
not: is written by staff before you answer any question

cards.subject: Your idea
says: is the first thing you give Moksy
is what the interview asks about
cards.use: are about to start a new Moksy project
not: must be a finished product before you can begin

cards.subject: Expert review
says: comes after the document has been generated
has a reviewer check the document
sits between the document and the build stage
cards.use: need the step where a person checks the generated plan
not: takes place before you answer the first interview question

cards.subject: The build stage
says: covers downloads, exports and hiring
comes after expert review
cards.use: want to download or export your finished plan
not: is the stage in which the AI asks its questions

cards.subject: Home
says: is the name of the customer home screen
is where a customer starts in the customer area
cards.use: want to find the first screen you land on as a customer
not: is the operator console that staff use

cards.subject: A customer
says: creates projects
receives documents
cards.use: are the person who types in an idea
not: checks other people's documents in the expert review

cards.subject: A reviewer
says: checks documents during expert review
is a different role from a customer
cards.use: need the person who checks a generated document
not: creates projects and receives the documents

cards.subject: The Console
says: is the operator console that staff use to run the platform
is not part of the customer area
cards.use: wonder which area staff use rather than customers
not: is the screen where customers manage their projects

cards.subject: A Moksy role
says: decides what a person can do on the platform
differs between customers, reviewers and staff
cards.use: wonder why two people see different things on the platform
not: is chosen by the colour theme of the account

cards.subject: MOX
says: stands for Moksy credit
is worth one cent each
is held in your Wallet
cards.use: want the unit that works like money on the platform
not: is a measure of experience used on the Ladder

cards.subject: MXP
says: stands for Moksy Experience Points
is what you climb the Ladder with
is experience rather than money
cards.use: want the unit that measures progress rather than money
not: is bought in packs and spent from the Wallet

cards.subject: The Wallet
says: holds your MOX
is where your MOX balance lives
cards.use: want to know where your credit is kept
not: is climbed with MXP

cards.subject: The Ladder
says: is climbed with MXP
measures experience rather than money
cards.use: want to know what MXP is used for
not: holds your MOX balance

cards.subject: Starter MOX
says: is granted when you join Moksy
is credit rather than experience
cards.use: wonder why a new account already has a balance
not: is earned only after your first review is finished

cards.subject: A MOX pack
says: is how you buy more MOX
adds credit to your Wallet
cards.use: run low on credit and want more
not: adds experience points to your Ladder

cards.subject: Escrow
says: holds MOX while a review is open
keeps credit set aside until the review finishes
cards.use: see your usable balance drop while a review is still running
not: converts your MOX into MXP

cards.subject: Pairing a unit with a noun
says: keeps MOX and MXP apart
means saying Wallet with MOX and Ladder with MXP
cards.use: worry about mixing up two marks that differ by one letter
not: is a legal rule that applies in every country

cards.subject: A balance of 250 MOX
says: equals 250 cents
is smaller than a balance of 1,000 MOX
cards.use: must convert a small Wallet balance to cents
not: equals 2,500 cents

cards.subject: A balance of 1,000 MOX
says: equals 1,000 cents
is four times a balance of 250 MOX
cards.use: must convert a larger Wallet balance to cents
not: equals 100 cents

cards.subject: A sourced figure
says: traces back to a stored fact with a source
can be explained when you ask where it came from
cards.use: want to know what makes a number in your document trustworthy
not: is any figure that looks reasonable to the writer

cards.subject: The writing model
says: may phrase a figure in plain words
never originates a number
cards.use: ask whether the AI may choose its own figures
not: is free to invent a plausible figure when none is stored

cards.subject: Your interview answers
says: are the input to your document
shape what the plan says about your idea
cards.use: want to know what the document is built from
not: are ignored when the document is written

cards.subject: Asking about a missing fact
says: hands the gap back to you as a question
avoids guessing by involving the person who knows
cards.use: see a question about something you did not mention
not: fills the gap silently with an estimate

cards.subject: Deriving a value
says: works a figure out from facts already stored
needs the underlying facts to be known first
cards.use: find a figure that was calculated rather than asked for
not: takes a number from the model's memory

cards.subject: Giving a range
says: shows a band with a low and a high figure
admits uncertainty instead of faking one exact number
cards.use: see a low-to-high figure in a place you expected one number
not: hides the uncertainty behind a single exact number

cards.subject: Refusing to state a figure
says: declines to give a number when no stored fact backs it
prefers an honest gap over an invented answer
cards.use: notice a section that says a number cannot be given
not: is a sign that your project has been deleted

cards.subject: The problem statement
says: says what pain or need your idea addresses
comes before any talk of features
cards.use: must explain why anyone would want your product
not: lists the technologies you plan to use

cards.subject: The target user
says: names the people who will use the product
lets the plan tailor features to a real audience
cards.use: are asked who the product is for
not: is the person who pays for hosting

cards.subject: The core feature
says: is the one capability without which the product is pointless
is what a first version must do well
cards.use: must name the single most important thing your product does
not: is the longest list of every feature you ever want

cards.subject: The success measure
says: states how you will know the product is working
is best expressed in numbers or observable events
cards.use: are asked how you would judge the product a success
not: is how good the logo looks

cards.subject: A constraint
says: is a limit such as budget, deadline or legal rule
narrows the options a plan can offer
cards.use: have a fixed launch date that the plan must respect
not: is a feature you want to add later

cards.subject: The budget range
says: tells the plan how much you can spend
helps rule out options that cost too much
cards.use: want the plan to propose only options you can afford
not: is the price the reviewer charges you

cards.subject: The platform choice
says: says whether the product is a website, a mobile app or both
changes the skills and cost of the build
cards.use: are asked where your users will use the product
not: is the colour palette of the product

cards.subject: A non-goal
says: names something you deliberately will not build in version one
protects the plan from drifting
cards.use: want to write down what is out of scope for now
not: is a goal that you plan to reach last

cards.subject: An alternative to your product
says: is what users do today without your product, even if that is nothing
shows what you must be better than
cards.use: are asked who or what you compete with
not: is only another company selling the same thing

cards.subject: A user journey
says: walks through the steps a user takes to reach their goal
reveals features that the idea forgot
cards.use: want to show how someone actually uses the product from start to finish
not: is the history of the founder's career

cards.subject: An assumption
says: is something you believe but have not yet verified
is worth testing early if the idea depends on it
cards.use: realise the plan depends on users paying for something you have not tested
not: is a fact backed by a stored source

cards.subject: A specific answer
says: gives concrete detail instead of a vague phrase
gives the document facts it can use
cards.use: are asked how busy your service will be
not: is a single general word such as good

cards.subject: A one-word answer
says: leaves the document with too little to work with
often forces the interview to ask again
cards.use: want to see why short replies make a weaker plan
not: gives the AI everything it needs

cards.subject: An honest answer
says: describes your real situation, even if it is unflattering
protects the plan from being built on wishful numbers
cards.use: are tempted to make your numbers sound better than they are
not: is one you shape to sound impressive

cards.subject: A numeric answer with units
says: states a quantity together with its unit, such as users per month
removes doubt about what a number means
cards.use: are asked how many orders you expect
not: is a bare number with nothing to say what it counts

cards.subject: Saying you do not know
says: tells the interview a gap exists so it can be handled
is better than guessing
cards.use: lack a figure that the interview asks for
not: makes the interview end immediately

cards.subject: Giving a real example
says: shows a typical case, such as one actual customer order
makes abstract needs concrete
cards.use: find it hard to describe a process in general terms
not: replaces the need to answer other questions

cards.subject: Mentioning constraints early
says: keeps the plan from offering options you cannot use
includes budget, deadlines and legal limits
cards.use: know of a regulation that will limit your product
not: should wait until after the document is delivered

cards.subject: Keeping answers consistent
says: avoids contradictions between earlier and later replies
prevents a plan that disagrees with itself
cards.use: notice that a later answer conflicts with an earlier one
not: means repeating the same sentence in every answer

cards.subject: Reviewing your answers before you finish
says: catches typos and wrong numbers before they reach the document
costs far less than correcting a finished plan
cards.use: are about to finish and want to avoid errors flowing downstream
not: is only needed when the reviewer asks for it

cards.subject: Pasting a long unrelated text
says: buries the relevant facts among noise
makes it harder to see what you actually need
cards.use: are tempted to paste an entire old report as one answer
not: always gives the AI more useful detail

cards.subject: A minimum viable product
says: contains only the features needed to test the core idea with real users
lets you learn before spending on everything
cards.use: want to test an idea cheaply with real people
not: includes every feature you ever want

cards.subject: A must-have feature
says: is essential for the product to work at all
belongs in the first release
cards.use: must decide what cannot be left out of version one
not: is a feature that would be pleasant but is not needed

cards.subject: A nice-to-have feature
says: adds value but is not essential
is the first thing to postpone when budget or time runs short
cards.use: must decide what can wait for a later release
not: must be built before anything else

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is the gradual growth of requirements after the plan is agreed
raises cost and delays delivery if left unmanaged
cards.use: see new feature requests arriving after the plan was signed off
not: is a smooth way to finish early

cards.subject: A user story
says: describes a need in the form as a user I want a goal so that a benefit
keeps a feature tied to a real person's need
cards.use: want to write a requirement from a user's point of view
not: is a technical diagram of the database

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: state testable conditions that decide whether a feature is done
let both sides agree on what finished means
cards.use: need an objective way to say a feature is complete
not: describe how the feature looks in the marketing page

cards.subject: A milestone
says: marks a checkable point in the project, such as a working login
gives you a moment to review progress
cards.use: want checkpoints along the way rather than one big handover
not: is the final invoice of the project

cards.subject: Phased delivery
says: ships the product in stages instead of all at once
lets feedback from early stages change later ones
cards.use: want to release the most valuable part first
not: waits for every feature before releasing anything

cards.subject: A prototype
says: is a rough, quickly built model used to test an idea
is usually thrown away or heavily reworked afterwards
cards.use: want to show a clickable concept before a full build
not: is the final production system

cards.subject: A dependency
says: is something your work needs from someone else before it can proceed
can delay a project even when your own tasks are on time
cards.use: learn that a feature cannot start until another party delivers
not: is a task that no one else cares about

cards.subject: A project risk
says: is something that might go wrong, with a likelihood and an impact
should be noted early so it can be reduced
cards.use: want to record what could derail the project
not: is a problem that has already happened and is solved

cards.subject: A change request
says: is a formal request to alter agreed scope
should be answered with its effect on cost and time
cards.use: want something added after the plan was agreed
not: is a complaint about the interview

cards.subject: The feature list
says: names what the product will do
is the part of a plan most people read first
cards.use: want to see what will actually be built
not: states how long the work will take

cards.subject: The tech stack
says: lists the languages, frameworks and services the build will use
affects which skills you must hire
cards.use: need to know which technologies the build depends on
not: lists the people who will use the product

cards.subject: The timeline
says: gives the order and duration of the work
shows when each milestone is expected
cards.use: want to know when you can expect the product
not: names the technologies chosen

cards.subject: The cost estimate
says: states what the build is expected to cost
is more honest as a range than as a single figure
cards.use: want to compare the plan against your budget
not: lists the user stories

cards.subject: The architecture overview
says: shows the main parts of the system and how they connect
helps a developer see the shape of the build
cards.use: want a high-level picture of how the product fits together
not: is a list of marketing channels

cards.subject: The risk register
says: lists risks with owners and ways to reduce them
gets reviewed as the project moves
cards.use: want to see what could go wrong and who watches it
not: lists the features in order of priority

cards.subject: The team and roles section
says: says who is needed, such as a designer and a developer
lets you plan hiring
cards.use: want to know which people the build requires
not: names the cloud provider

cards.subject: The testing plan
says: says how you will check the product works before launch
covers what is tested and who tests it
cards.use: want to know how quality will be checked
not: lists risks with owners

cards.subject: The integrations list
says: names outside services the product connects to, such as payments or email
shows what you depend on from other providers
cards.use: want to know which third-party services are involved
not: describes the screens a user sees

cards.subject: The data model
says: describes what information is stored and how the pieces relate
drives how the database is designed
cards.use: want to understand what the product remembers about users and their activity
not: is the colour system of the interface

cards.subject: The non-functional requirements
says: cover qualities such as speed, availability and security
describe how well the product works rather than what it does
cards.use: must say how fast and how reliable the product has to be
not: are the features users see

cards.subject: The launch plan
says: says how the product reaches its first users
covers rollout, support and how to roll back
cards.use: want to know what happens on the day the product goes live
not: is the list of tests run during development

cards.subject: A range estimate
says: gives a low and a high figure
reflects uncertainty honestly
cards.use: are given a cost that shows a minimum and a maximum
not: promises an exact final price

cards.subject: A contingency buffer
says: is extra time or money set aside for the unexpected
is added on top of the base estimate
cards.use: want to plan for surprises
not: is the profit margin of the supplier

cards.subject: Building from scratch
says: writes the software as custom code
gives the most freedom but usually takes the longest
cards.use: need a product that no existing software can provide
not: reuses a ready-made product with little change

cards.subject: A rebuild
says: replaces an existing system with new software
uses the old system as a reference for what is needed
cards.use: already run an old system that you want to modernise
not: starts with no existing system to learn from

cards.subject: An open-source option
says: uses software whose code is public and often free to license
leaves support and upkeep largely to you or a hired expert
cards.use: want software you can inspect and change without licence fees
not: comes with a vendor who guarantees support as part of a fee

cards.subject: A closed-source option
says: uses commercial software whose code you cannot change
typically comes with licence fees and vendor support
cards.use: prefer a supported product from a vendor over self-maintained software
not: lets anyone read and modify the code freely

cards.subject: The hybrid approach
says: combines bought or open parts with custom code
spends custom effort only where you need to differ
cards.use: want ready-made parts for common features and custom code for what is unique
not: builds every part from scratch

cards.subject: Total cost of ownership
says: counts running costs such as hosting, upkeep and licences
covers the whole life of the product, not only the build
cards.use: compare two options and want to include what happens after launch
not: is the price of the first invoice only

cards.subject: Vendor lock-in
says: makes switching away from a supplier costly
grows when your data and workflows depend on one provider
cards.use: worry that moving off a product later would be hard
not: guarantees the lowest long-term price

cards.subject: Ongoing maintenance
says: keeps the product working after launch
continues to cost money and time every year
cards.use: wonder who pays to fix and update the product once it is live
not: ends on the day of launch

cards.subject: A fixed-price contract
says: sets the total price up front
handles changes through formal change requests
cards.use: want to know the total price before work begins
not: bills for every hour regardless of agreed scope

cards.subject: A time-and-materials contract
says: bills for the time and resources actually used
lets the final cost grow if the scope grows
cards.use: expect the scope to change as you learn
not: fixes the total price before work starts

cards.subject: Reading the whole document first
says: gives you the full picture before judging a section
stops you from objecting to something explained later
cards.use: have just received your document and want to start well
not: means skipping straight to the cost estimate

cards.subject: Checking it against your goal
says: compares each section with your problem statement
shows whether the plan solves your actual problem
cards.use: want to know whether the plan fits what you set out to do
not: only checks spelling and grammar

cards.subject: Checking the numbers
says: asks where each figure comes from
spots figures that no source supports
cards.use: see a cost or date and want to trust it
not: accepts any figure that is formatted neatly

cards.subject: Questioning every assumption
says: asks what must be true for the plan to hold
uncovers hidden risks
cards.use: suspect the plan relies on something nobody has verified
not: assumes that a confident tone means certainty

cards.subject: Asking a clarifying question
says: points to the unclear section and asks a specific thing
gets better answers than a general complaint
cards.use: do not understand a part of your document
not: says only that the document is bad

cards.subject: Checking for missing sections
says: compares the document with what a plan normally covers
finds gaps such as no testing plan or no risks
cards.use: feel that something important seems absent
not: counts only the pages in the document

cards.subject: Separating must-fix from preference
says: marks which issues are errors and which are matters of taste
keeps feedback focused on what matters
cards.use: have a long list of comments and limited time
not: treats every comment as equally urgent

cards.subject: Keeping dated copies
says: lets you see what changed between versions
avoids confusion over which version is current
cards.use: receive several revisions of a document
not: is unnecessary if you trust your memory

cards.subject: Involving the decision maker
says: has the person with budget authority read before the build starts
avoids rework after approval
cards.use: know that someone else must approve the spend
not: is only needed after the product has launched

cards.subject: Not approving under pressure
says: takes time even when someone urges a quick yes
reduces the cost of mistakes found late
cards.use: feel rushed to sign off a plan
not: treats speed as the most important thing

cards.subject: Testing the plan against your constraints
says: checks cost, time and skills against the limits you gave
reveals options that you cannot actually use
cards.use: want to see whether you can afford and staff the plan
not: ignores your budget and deadline

cards.subject: A written brief
says: gives a developer the same information the plan holds
reduces misunderstandings before work starts
cards.use: want to explain the work clearly to someone you may hire
not: is a verbal summary on a call

cards.subject: A portfolio check
says: looks at past work similar to yours
gives evidence beyond what a candidate claims
cards.use: want proof that a candidate has built something like your product
not: relies on how confident the candidate sounds

cards.subject: References
says: let you hear from previous clients about reliability
help confirm what a portfolio shows
cards.use: want to ask previous clients how a candidate behaved
not: are copies of the candidate's certificates

cards.subject: A trial task
says: is a small, paid piece of work done before a larger commitment
shows how a candidate works and communicates
cards.use: are unsure about a candidate and want a low-risk test
not: is a long unpaid project

cards.subject: A written contract
says: records scope, price and deadlines
gives both sides something to refer to when they disagree
cards.use: are about to agree on work with a developer
not: is unnecessary if you trust each other

cards.subject: Milestone payments
says: release money as defined stages are completed
keep payment tied to delivered progress
cards.use: want to avoid paying everything before work is done
not: require the full price on day one

cards.subject: Ownership of the work
says: states who owns the code and designs once they are delivered
should be settled in writing before work starts
cards.use: want to be sure you keep the product after the contract ends
not: passes to the developer by default in every case

cards.subject: A non-disclosure agreement
says: binds the other side to keep your information confidential
is signed before you share sensitive details
cards.use: must share your idea in detail with someone you do not know yet
not: transfers ownership of the product

cards.subject: Least-privilege access
says: gives a contractor only the access their work needs
is withdrawn when the work ends
cards.use: must give a new developer access to your accounts and systems
not: gives everyone full administrator rights from the start

cards.subject: A communication rhythm
says: sets regular updates such as a weekly check-in
brings problems to light early
cards.use: want to know how work is going without chasing
not: waits until the end for any news

cards.subject: Handover documentation
says: lets you or another developer run and change the product later
should be delivered along with the code
cards.use: want to avoid being stuck if the developer leaves
not: is optional when the code works on the day of delivery

cards.subject: A strong unique password
says: is long and hard to guess
is not reused on any other service
cards.use: are creating a password for your Moksy account
not: is a short word you can easily remember

cards.subject: A password manager
says: stores a different strong password for each service
fills passwords in so you need not remember them
cards.use: have too many accounts to remember passwords for
not: keeps all your accounts safe by using one password everywhere

cards.subject: Two-factor authentication
says: asks for a second proof such as a code from your phone
protects the account even if the password leaks
cards.use: want an extra lock on your account
not: replaces your password with a shorter one

cards.subject: A phishing message
says: imitates a trusted sender to steal your details
often creates urgency or fear
cards.use: receive an email that demands you log in at once or lose access
not: is a normal notice from a real service

cards.subject: Checking the web address
says: confirms you are on the real site before you type a password
spots lookalike domains
cards.use: are about to enter your login after clicking a link
not: is unnecessary when the page looks familiar

cards.subject: Keeping your credentials private
says: means you never give your password to anyone, including support
applies to codes sent to your phone
cards.use: are asked by a message to send your password or code
not: is relaxed when the sender says they work for support

cards.subject: Logging out on shared devices
says: ends your session so the next person cannot use it
matters most on public computers
cards.use: used a library or office computer to check your account
not: is unnecessary if you close the browser tab

cards.subject: A current recovery email
says: lets you regain access if you lose your password
should be an address only you control
cards.use: want to be able to reset a forgotten password
not: can be an old address you no longer read

cards.subject: Paying only inside the platform
says: keeps payments recorded and traceable
avoids scams that move you to private channels
cards.use: are asked by a stranger to pay through a private link
not: is optional if the other side seems friendly

cards.subject: Reviewing account activity
says: helps you spot logins or changes you did not make
lets you react before damage grows
cards.use: suspect that someone else may have used your account
not: is only needed once a year

cards.subject: Using public Wi-Fi
says: can expose your traffic to others on the network
is safer for logins when the site uses HTTPS
cards.use: must check your account from a cafe
not: is always as safe as your home network

cards.subject: Respectful feedback
says: criticises the work and not the person
keeps conversations with reviewers productive
cards.use: disagree with a comment from a reviewer
not: uses insults when you are frustrated

cards.subject: Honest information
says: describes your idea and situation truthfully
keeps the plan and the review reliable
cards.use: are tempted to exaggerate your idea to get a better result
not: is optional when you are in a hurry

cards.subject: Lawful ideas
says: means submitting only ideas that are legal
is a basic expectation on platforms like Moksy
cards.use: consider describing an idea that breaks the law
not: is waived if the idea is only for testing

cards.subject: Protecting personal data
says: keeps real people's private details out of your idea text
uses made-up examples instead of real records
cards.use: want to explain a process that normally handles customer records
not: means pasting a real customer list into an answer

cards.subject: Third-party confidential material
says: means not sharing secrets that belong to someone else
includes documents covered by an agreement you signed
cards.use: hold an employer's internal documents that describe your idea
not: is allowed because you have access to the files

cards.subject: Respecting intellectual property
says: means not claiming work that belongs to others
includes code, text and designs
cards.use: want to copy another company's text into your plan
not: is waived when you change a few words

cards.subject: Fair, clear requests
says: ask reviewers for reasonable work in clear terms
respect the time of the person reviewing
cards.use: must brief a reviewer on what you need checked
not: demand unlimited changes for a single review

cards.subject: One account per person
says: keeps balances, history and accountability on one identity
reduces abuse of free starter credit
cards.use: wonder why a platform restricts duplicate accounts
not: is a rule that exists only for staff

cards.subject: Using credit as intended
says: spends credit on the services it is meant for
avoids exploiting loopholes
cards.use: discover a trick that gives free credit
not: is satisfied by using any loophole you find

cards.subject: Reporting a bug rather than exploiting it
says: tells the platform about a flaw you stumble upon
protects other users and your own standing
cards.use: notice that your balance was credited in error
not: means keeping the mistake quiet and spending it

cards.subject: Reading the in-product hint
says: answers common questions on the spot
is the quickest first step when something is unclear
cards.use: see a field or message you do not understand
not: is only meant for staff

cards.subject: Searching the help guides
says: finds written answers to common questions
is worth doing before contacting support
cards.use: have a how-do-I question
not: replaces any need to describe your problem

cards.subject: Describing expected and actual results
says: says what you thought would happen and what happened instead
gives support the gap to investigate
cards.use: are about to report that something does not work
not: says only that it is broken

cards.subject: Listing the steps to reproduce
says: gives the exact actions that lead to the problem
lets support see the issue for themselves
cards.use: hit a problem that does not happen every time
not: leaves out the actions because they seem obvious

cards.subject: Quoting the exact error message
says: gives support the precise words the system showed
is more useful than a paraphrase
cards.use: see an error pop up on screen
not: is replaced by saying it showed an error

cards.subject: Attaching a screenshot
says: shows what you saw at the moment of the problem
is best when personal data is hidden
cards.use: cannot explain a layout problem in words
not: should show your password field with the password visible

cards.subject: Naming the project concerned
says: tells support which project is affected
saves them a round of questions
cards.use: have several projects and a problem with only one of them
not: is unnecessary when you only wrote in a hurry

cards.subject: One issue per request
says: keeps each problem easy to track and answer
avoids parts of a message being missed
cards.use: have three unrelated questions for support
not: is the reason to bundle everything into one long message

cards.subject: Stating the impact and urgency
says: says how much the problem affects you and by when you need it
helps support decide what to handle first
cards.use: face a deadline that the problem threatens
not: is replaced by writing in capital letters

cards.subject: Never sending a password to support
says: keeps your account safe even from imposters
is a rule that holds even when the request looks official
cards.use: are asked to include your password in a support message
not: speeds up the help you get

cards.subject: Replying in the same thread
says: keeps the history of the problem together
lets any support person catch up quickly
cards.use: want to add information to a request you already sent
not: means opening a new request each time

qa.q: What does Moksy do?
qa.right: Turns an idea into a build-ready plan
qa.why: Moksy turns an idea into a build-ready plan.

qa.q: Where do you keep one idea and its document in Moksy?
qa.right: In a project
qa.why: One idea and its document live in a project.

qa.q: Where do you see your MOX balance?
qa.right: In your Wallet
qa.why: The Wallet holds MOX.

qa.q: How much is 1 MOX worth?
qa.right: One cent
qa.why: 1 MOX equals one cent.

qa.q: What does the AI do in the interview?
qa.right: Asks questions about your idea
qa.why: The interview gathers your answers.

qa.q: Which is the best way to protect your Moksy account?
qa.right: Use a long unique password that you do not reuse
wrong: Use your name as the password
Reuse your email password so you remember it
Share the password with a colleague to be safe
qa.why: Unique strong passwords limit the damage if one leaks.

qa.q: When something on screen is unclear, what is a good first step?
qa.right: Read the hint or help guide on the screen
wrong: Delete the project and start again
Wait a week and hope it changes
qa.why: Built-in hints and guides answer many questions quickly.

qa.q: What is the order of the Moksy journey?
qa.right: Idea, interview, document, expert review, build
qa.why: The document comes from the interview and is checked before building.

qa.q: What do you receive when you join Moksy?
qa.right: Starter MOX
qa.why: New accounts receive Starter MOX.

qa.q: Which pairing is correct?
qa.right: MOX in the Wallet, MXP on the Ladder
wrong: MXP in the Wallet, MOX on the Ladder
qa.why: MOX is credit and MXP is experience.

qa.q: Which answer is better for an interview question about expected traffic?
qa.right: About 300 orders a week, mostly on weekends
qa.why: A specific number with a unit gives the document something to use.

qa.q: What does the expert review do?
qa.right: A reviewer checks your document
qa.why: Reviewers check documents.

qa.q: Which email is most likely phishing?
qa.right: One that says your account will be closed in an hour unless you log in through its link
wrong: One that thanks you for a purchase you made and shows no link to click
A notice that arrives after you asked to reset your password
A message from your own contact list that you were expecting
qa.why: Urgency and a login link are classic phishing signs.

qa.q: How should you share a screenshot with support?
qa.right: After hiding any personal data in it
wrong: With your password visible so they can check
Only after cropping out the error
By describing it instead, never as an image
qa.why: Screenshots help, but should not expose secrets.

qa.q: Which is a good reason to use two-factor authentication?
qa.right: The account stays protected if the password leaks
wrong: It lets you skip the password
qa.why: A second factor blocks someone who only has the password.

qa.q: What happens to MOX while a review of your document is open?
qa.right: It is held in escrow
qa.why: Escrow holds MOX until the review finishes.

qa.q: What is the build stage for?
qa.right: Downloads, exports and hiring
qa.why: Build is what you do with the finished plan.

qa.q: Your Wallet balance seems lower while a review is open. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: Some MOX is held in escrow until the review finishes
qa.why: MOX is held in escrow while a review is open.

qa.q: A friend says you buy MXP in packs. What do you tell them?
qa.right: MOX is what you buy in packs; MXP is experience for the Ladder
wrong: MOX and MXP are the same
qa.why: Money and experience are different things.

qa.q: Your document contains a figure with no source behind it. What does Moksy's rule say should be true?
qa.right: Every figure should trace to a stored fact with a source
wrong: Unsourced figures are fine if they look right
qa.why: A model may phrase a figure but may not originate one.

qa.q: Moksy lacks a fact it needs. What does it do rather than invent a number?
qa.right: It asks, derives the value or gives a range
wrong: It makes up a plausible figure
qa.why: Missing facts lead to a question, a derivation or a band.

qa.q: Which interview answer helps the document most?
qa.right: Specific, honest answers about your idea
qa.why: The document is built from your answers.

qa.q: A developer you want to hire asks about your plan. What should you give them first?
qa.right: A written brief based on the document
wrong: Your account password so they can read it
qa.why: A written brief reduces misunderstandings and does not require credentials.

qa.q: You need to report a problem to support. Which message is most useful?
qa.right: "When I click Export on project Shop App, I expected a file but saw the message 'Export failed'."
qa.why: Expected result, actual result and the project help support act.

qa.q: A trial task before hiring a developer is best described as which?
qa.right: A small paid piece of work that shows how they work
qa.why: A trial task limits risk for both sides.

qa.q: Which is the best use of the review stage?
qa.right: Check the document against your goals before you start the build
wrong: Approve whatever the first reader says
qa.why: The review is your chance to catch problems before money is spent.

qa.q: Support asks you to send your password to confirm who you are. What should you do?
qa.right: Refuse; real support never needs your password
qa.why: Passwords are never shared, even with support.

qa.q: You want to tell a reviewer that a section is wrong. What is best?
qa.right: Point to the section and say what is wrong and why
wrong: Say the whole document is poor
qa.why: Specific and polite feedback is easier to act on.

qa.q: Your Wallet shows 250 MOX. What is it worth?
qa.right: 250 cents
qa.why: 1 MOX is one cent.

qa.q: You want to climb the Ladder. Which do you earn?
qa.right: MXP
qa.why: The Ladder runs on MXP.

qa.q: Your document gives a cost as a range of 8,000 to 12,000. How should you read it?
qa.right: As an honest sign of uncertainty with a low and a high end
wrong: As a mistake in the document
As the amount you owe in MOX
qa.why: A range admits uncertainty rather than faking precision.

qa.q: The plan is complete but your budget is lower than its cost. What should you do first?
qa.right: Ask which features are must-haves and which can wait for later releases
wrong: Hire the cheapest developer you can find
qa.why: Prioritising scope is the safest way to fit a budget.

qa.q: New feature requests keep arriving after you approved the plan. What is the safest response?
qa.right: Treat each as a change request and ask for its effect on cost and time
wrong: Skip the effect on cost to save time
qa.why: Change requests keep scope under control.

qa.q: You are given the choice between a fixed-price and a time-and-materials contract, and your requirements are still uncertain. Which fits better?
qa.right: Time and materials, because the scope may change
wrong: Fixed price, because it removes all risk
Neither, because no contract is needed
Fixed price, because change is free
qa.why: A fixed price assumes stable scope; changes are costly.

qa.q: A contractor you just met asks for payment outside the platform. What should you do?
qa.right: Decline and keep payments traceable
wrong: Pay half now to build trust
Send the money to a personal account
Pay in full if they promise quickly
qa.why: Off-platform payments are a common scam pattern.

qa.q: You notice your Wallet was credited more than you paid. What is the right thing to do?
qa.right: Tell the platform about the error
wrong: Ignore it and open a second account
qa.why: Reporting protects you and others.

qa.q: Your plan says the product will use a particular paid service. What should you check before accepting it?
qa.right: Its ongoing costs and how hard it would be to switch away
wrong: Only the colour of its logo
qa.why: Total cost and lock-in matter beyond the first price.

qa.q: You will use a contractor's code for years. Which should be settled in writing?
qa.right: Who owns the code and designs after delivery
qa.why: Ownership is a classic dispute if left unsaid.

qa.q: You sign in on a library computer. What should you do when you finish?
qa.right: Log out of your account
wrong: Leave it signed in for the next visit
Save the password in the browser
qa.why: A session left open lets the next person act as you.

qa.q: The interview asks for a number you do not have. What is best?
qa.right: Say you do not know so the gap can be handled
wrong: End the interview and start another
qa.why: A guess poisons the plan; a stated gap can be handled.

qa.q: Two answers you gave now contradict each other. What should you do?
qa.right: Correct the answer that is wrong before finishing
wrong: Leave both because the AI will choose
qa.why: Consistent answers produce a coherent plan.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the units correctly?
qa.right: I topped up my Wallet with MOX and I earn MXP on the Ladder
wrong: I topped up my Wallet with MXP and I earn MOX on the Ladder
I climb the Wallet with MOX
My Ladder holds 300 MOX of experience
qa.why: Wallet goes with MOX and Ladder with MXP.

qa.q: Which statement about MOX and MXP is correct?
qa.right: 1 MOX is one cent; MXP is experience points and not money
wrong: MXP can be spent in the Wallet
MOX is used to climb the Ladder
qa.why: Money and experience are separate.

qa.q: Who is allowed to originate a figure in a Moksy document?
qa.right: Nobody: a model may phrase a figure but only stored facts supply it
qa.why: Figures come from stored data with a source.

qa.q: You find one figure in your document that you know is wrong. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Point to the figure, say what you know and ask where the document's number came from
wrong: Ignore it because it is only one figure
Approve the document and fix it during the build
qa.why: Naming the figure and asking for its source is the right route.

qa.q: A reviewer's comment contradicts your goal. What do you do?
qa.right: Ask a clarifying question and explain your goal
qa.why: Clarify first; many disagreements are misunderstandings.

qa.q: Your launch date is fixed. Which approach protects it best?
qa.right: Phased delivery of the must-haves first, with extras later
wrong: Adding every feature to the first release
qa.why: Prioritising keeps a date realistic.

qa.q: A message pretends to be from Moksy and links to a login page with a slightly different address. What do you do?
qa.right: Do not log in there; go to the site by typing the address yourself
wrong: Reply with a password to verify
Forward it to all your contacts
qa.why: Lookalike domains are a hallmark of phishing.

qa.q: A developer cannot start until another team delivers an item. What is that item?
qa.right: A dependency
qa.why: Work waiting on someone else is a dependency.

qa.q: A support request mentions three separate problems in a single long message. What is the likely result?
qa.right: Parts of it are overlooked or delayed
wrong: Support fixes only the first and closes the request
qa.why: One issue per request keeps tracking simple.

qa.q: You are asked to paste real customer records into the interview to describe your process. What should you do?
qa.right: Use made-up examples that show the same pattern
wrong: Paste the records, since the AI needs them
qa.why: Private data of others should stay out.

qa.q: A developer you hired asks for administrator access to everything. What do you do?
qa.right: Give only the access their tasks need and remove it at the end
wrong: Give full access to be quick
qa.why: Least privilege limits damage and risk.

qa.q: Which statement shows an honest handling of uncertainty in a plan?
qa.right: Cost is likely between 8,000 and 12,000, depending on whether we buy or build the login
qa.why: A range with its driver is honest and useful.

qa.q: After approving the plan you realise the testing plan is missing. What is the best move?
qa.right: Ask for it to be added before the build starts
wrong: Assume the developer will test everything
qa.why: Gaps are cheapest to close before building.

qa.q: A project's result depends on a number you assumed but never checked. How should you treat it?
qa.right: As an assumption to verify early
qa.why: Unverified beliefs are assumptions and carry risk.

qa.q: Which is a good success measure for a booking app?
qa.right: Fifty paid bookings in the first month
qa.why: Good measures are numbers or observable events.

qa.q: Which of these belongs in a good idea description?
qa.right: The problem and who has it
qa.why: A clear problem and user anchor the plan.

qa.q: A section of your plan names no risks at all. What should you conclude?
qa.right: A risk list is missing and should be requested
wrong: Risks are the reviewer's concern, not yours
qa.why: Every project has risks; missing sections should be requested.

qa.q: You agree to milestone payments. When should you release each payment?
qa.right: When the agreed milestone has been delivered and checked
wrong: At the end of the project
qa.why: Payment tied to checked progress limits risk.

qa.q: Which is the right way to give feedback to a reviewer you disagree with?
qa.right: Calmly describe your point and the reason
qa.why: Respectful feedback keeps the process productive.
